title: Expected Value & Conditional Probability
tagline: The single most important math for any quant interview — think in expected value, fast and correctly.

concept.analogy: Expected value is the 'fair price' of a gamble. If a game pays $10 on heads and costs you $4 on tails, a fair coin makes it worth (½·$10) + (½·−$4) = $3 per play on average. A trader's whole job is finding bets whose price is below their expected value and taking them repeatedly — exactly what a casino does, just with the edge on your side.
paragraphs: Expected value (EV) is the probability-weighted average of all outcomes: EV = Σ (probability of outcome × value of outcome). It's the foundation of quant trading because every trade is a bet, and you want positive-EV bets you can repeat. By the law of large numbers, repeating a positive-EV bet many times converts that edge into near-certain profit.

Conditional probability — P(A | B), the probability of A given that B happened — is the other pillar. It's defined as P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It captures how new information updates probabilities, and it's where most people's intuition breaks (the Monty Hall problem, the two-children problem, base-rate fallacies). Interviewers love these because they reveal whether you actually reason or just pattern-match.

Two tools you'll use constantly: linearity of expectation — E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always, even when X and Y are dependent — which turns scary problems into easy sums; and indicator variables — write a count as a sum of 0/1 indicators and take expectations. Many 'hard' problems collapse instantly with these.

The interview skill isn't just knowing formulas — it's setting up the right model fast, computing cleanly under pressure, and narrating your reasoning so the interviewer follows your logic. Calibration (knowing how confident to be) matters as much as the final number.
points: EV = Σ probability × value; positive-EV bets, repeated, become near-certain profit.
Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) — how information updates probability.
Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y], even for dependent variables.
Indicator variables turn counts into sums of expectations — a superpower for hard problems.
The skill is fast, clean setup + narration, not memorized formulas.
concept.keyIdea: Think in expected value, and use linearity of expectation + indicator variables to make hard counting/probability problems easy. Conditional probability is where intuition fails — slow down and use the definition.

deepDive.intro: Let's build the toolkit with the exact techniques that crack interview problems.

steps.title: Computing EV cleanly
steps.detail: List outcomes, attach probabilities (they must sum to 1), multiply and sum. For a fair die, E[roll] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. For a bet, include the cost: net EV = EV of payoff − cost. You take the bet iff net EV > 0 (ignoring risk/variance, which matters for sizing).

steps.title: Linearity of expectation
steps.detail: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] regardless of dependence. Example: expected number of heads in 100 flips = sum of E[indicator each flip is heads] = 100 × ½ = 50. Example: expected fixed points of a random permutation = n × (1/n) = 1, no matter n — each position is a fixed point with prob 1/n, and you just add them.

steps.title: Indicator variables
steps.detail: To find E[count of something], define X_i = 1 if condition i holds, else 0; then count = Σ X_i and E[count] = Σ P(condition i). This sidesteps complicated dependence. Most 'expected number of ___' problems are one line with this trick.

steps.title: Conditional probability and the definition
steps.detail: Always fall back to P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B). The two-children problem: given at least one boy, P(both boys)? Outcomes {BB, BG, GB} are equally likely among those with ≥1 boy, so 1/3, not 1/2 — the conditioning changed the sample space. Drawing the sample space beats intuition.

steps.title: Law of total probability
steps.detail: P(A) = Σ P(A | B_i)·P(B_i) over a partition {B_i}. Useful when an outcome depends on a hidden state: average the conditional probabilities, weighted by how likely each state is. This is also the setup for Bayes' theorem (next lesson).

notes.title: Variance and why traders care
notes.detail: EV tells you the long-run average; variance tells you the bumpiness. Two positive-EV bets can need very different sizing — a high-variance bet can bankrupt you before the edge materializes. This is why position sizing (e.g., Kelly criterion) and risk limits exist. Interviewers often follow an EV question with 'how much would you bet?'

pitfalls: Forgetting the cost when computing a bet's net EV.
Assuming independence when events are dependent (or vice versa) — check.
Conditional-probability errors: not updating the sample space when you condition on information.
Confusing EV with certainty — a positive-EV bet can still lose; size for variance.

practice.intro: These are representative of the rapid-fire probability questions that open trader/research interviews. Try each fully before revealing.

interviewQuestions.q: You roll a fair die once. You win its value in dollars, but you may, before rolling, choose to instead reroll once and take the second value. What's the optimal strategy and the game's expected value?
a: If allowed to reroll after seeing the first roll: you should reroll whenever the first roll is below the expected value of a fresh roll (3.5), i.e., reroll on 1, 2, or 3; keep 4, 5, 6.

EV = P(first ≥ 4)·E[first | ≥4] + P(first ≤ 3)·E[fresh roll]. P(first ≥ 4) = 1/2 with mean 5; P(first ≤ 3) = 1/2, then you reroll for mean 3.5. EV = ½·5 + ½·3.5 = 2.5 + 1.75 = 4.25. (Contrast: no reroll option = 3.5.)
followups: What if you get two rerolls?
What's the value of the option to reroll?

interviewQuestions.q: A family has two children. Given that at least one is a boy, what's the probability both are boys?
a: Equally likely birth orders are BB, BG, GB, GG. Conditioning on 'at least one boy' removes GG, leaving {BB, BG, GB}, each equally likely.

Among these, only BB has both boys, so P(both boys | at least one boy) = 1/3 — not 1/2. The information shrank and reshaped the sample space. (Note: a subtly different phrasing — 'the older child is a boy' — gives 1/2, which is why precise conditioning matters.)

interviewQuestions.q: What is the expected number of die rolls to get the first 6?
a: This is a geometric distribution with success probability p = 1/6. The expected number of trials until the first success is 1/p.
So E[rolls] = 1/(1/6) = 6. Intuition/derivation: let E be the answer; with prob 1/6 you're done in 1 roll, with prob 5/6 you've used a roll and start over: E = 1 + (5/6)E ⇒ (1/6)E = 1 ⇒ E = 6.

interviewQuestions.q: Shuffle a deck of 52 cards uniformly at random. What is the expected number of cards in their original position?
a: Use indicator variables: let X_i = 1 if card i is in its original position. The expected count is E[Σ X_i] = Σ P(card i in original position) by linearity of expectation (which holds despite the positions being dependent).

Each card is equally likely to be in any of the 52 positions, so P(card i in its original spot) = 1/52. Summing over 52 cards: E = 52 × (1/52) = 1. Remarkably, the answer is 1 regardless of deck size n.

interviewQuestions.q: Why is linearity of expectation so powerful, and what's a common misconception about it?
a: Linearity of expectation says E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] for ANY random variables, full stop. Its power is that it holds *even when the variables are dependent* — so you can decompose a complicated quantity (often via indicator variables, one per event) into a sum of simple expectations and add them up, completely sidestepping the joint distribution and any messy dependence.

The common misconception is that you need independence to add expectations — you don't (that's required for things like Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y) or E[XY]=E[X]E[Y], not for E[X+Y]). This trips up candidates on problems like expected fixed points of a permutation, expected number of records, or coupon-collector stages, where the events are clearly dependent yet linearity still gives the answer in one line. Recognizing 'sum of indicators + linearity' is one of the highest-leverage tools in quant interviews.
followups: Give an example where dependence matters (variance) but not for expectation.
How do indicator variables formalize this?

problems.title: Expected rolls to see all six faces
problems.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die repeatedly. What is the expected number of rolls until you've seen all six faces at least once? Solve it and explain the method (a classic 'coupon collector' linearity-of-expectation problem).
problems.hint: Break into stages: time to get the k-th new face once you have k-1. Each stage is geometric.
problems.tests: Linearity of expectation + geometric waiting times.

approach: Use linearity of expectation by splitting into stages. Let T_k be the number of rolls to get the k-th distinct face after you already have k−1 distinct faces. When you have k−1 faces, the probability a roll gives a new face is (6−(k−1))/6, so T_k is geometric with that success probability and E[T_k] = 6/(6−(k−1)).

So E[T] = 6 × 2.45 = 14.7 rolls. The method generalizes: for n coupons it's n·H_n ≈ n·ln n, which interviewers love because it shows linearity of expectation turning a scary 'until all collected' question into a sum of easy geometric stages.

problems.title: Expected number of fixed points
problems.statement: n people throw their hats into a pile and each picks one back at random (a uniformly random permutation). What is the expected number of people who get their own hat back? Solve with indicator variables and explain why the answer is surprisingly simple.
problems.hint: Define an indicator for each person getting their own hat; use linearity (no independence needed).

approach: Let X_i = 1 if person i gets their own hat, else 0. The number of fixed points is X = Σ X_i. By linearity of expectation, E[X] = Σ E[X_i] — and linearity holds even though the X_i are NOT independent (knowing one person got their hat changes the others' probabilities), which is the key insight.
For a uniformly random permutation, person i is equally likely to receive any of the n hats, so P(X_i=1) = 1/n, hence E[X_i] = 1/n. Therefore E[X] = n × (1/n) = 1.

The expected number of fixed points is exactly 1, regardless of n. It's a classic demonstration that linearity of expectation lets you avoid the messy dependence structure of permutations entirely — a tool interviewers test constantly because candidates wrongly think they need independence.

problems.title: Should you play this dice game?
problems.statement: A game: roll one fair die; you're paid the number shown in dollars, but it costs $4 to play. Compute the expected profit per play and decide whether to play. Then: you may instead pay $1 to re-roll once and keep the second roll if you wish (you choose optimally). What's the optimal re-roll policy and the new expected value?
problems.hint: EV of one die = 3.5. For the re-roll, only re-roll when the first roll is below the EV of a fresh roll.

approach: Base game: E[payout] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. Cost $4, so expected profit = 3.5 − 4 = −$0.50 per play. Don't play the base game — it's a negative-EV bet.

With the optional $1 re-roll: you should re-roll only when your first roll is worse than the expected value of a fresh roll (3.5), i.e., re-roll on a 1, 2, or 3; keep a 4, 5, or 6. Expected payout = P(keep)·E[kept] + P(reroll)·E[fresh]. Keep happens for {4,5,6} (prob 1/2) with average 5; re-roll for {1,2,3} (prob 1/2) giving a fresh die worth 3.5 on average. So E[payout] = ½·5 + ½·3.5 = 2.5 + 1.75 = 4.25.

Net with re-roll cost: you pay $4 to play and, when you re-roll (half the time), an extra $1, so expected re-roll cost = ½·$1 = $0.50. Expected profit = 4.25 − 4 − 0.50 = −$0.25. Still negative — the re-roll improved EV (from −0.50 to −0.25) but not enough to make the game worth playing. The lesson: compute EV, use the 'only re-roll below the mean' optimal-stopping rule, and don't take negative-EV bets even when an option improves them.
